label: cruciform
reason: This is the standard glossary meaning (four arms at right angles, e.g. Brassicaceae corollas and cross-shaped hairs). PATO has no cruciform term; PATO:0001953 decussate is about leaf arrangement, not outline. The synonyms fit.

label: tunicate
reason: The definition is correct for bulbs and corms with tunics, and PATO has no such term. FLOPO already has the part 'tunic' (FLOPO:0986041), so a has-part rule could also express this. The class itself is sound.

label: horn-shaped
definition: A 3-D shape quality inhering in a bearer by virtue of the bearer's being elongated, tapering to a point and usually curved, like an animal horn.
reason: Wrong parent. A curved, tapering horn is not a convex 3-D shape in PATO's sense, because a line between two points can fall outside the object. The general PATO:0002266 '3-D shape' fits. The definition text is otherwise fine.

label: urticating
definition: A structural quality inhering in a bearer by virtue of the bearer's being a stiff hair with a brittle, easily broken tip that, on contact, breaks off and injects an irritant fluid into the skin.
reason: The current text has two bearers: the hair, plus 'said of a plant or part that bears such hairs'. A plant or leaf that is urticating should be expressed as having urticating trichomes (has-part), not by the same quality. The meaning for hairs is right.

label: coronate
definition: A shape quality inhering in a bearer by virtue of the bearer's bearing at its apex a crown, a short ring-like rim or circle of small teeth, scales or bristles, often formed by a persistent calyx limb or pappus.
reason: The 'crowned' sense (e.g. achenes or fruits topped by a persistent calyx rim) is right, and the rewrite only makes the crown's makeup clearer. When the pappus itself is called coronate, it means the pappus is crown-shaped. That should go to PATO:0040006 'crown like', not to this class.

label: abruptly narrowed
reason: The synonym 'contracted' does not fit as an exact synonym. In floras 'contracted' mostly means a dense, narrow inflorescence (e.g. a contracted panicle) or shortened, not a sudden narrowing of a blade. Make it at most a related synonym and keep 'abruptly contracted' and 'brusquement rétréci' as exact. The definition itself is fine.

label: saxicolous
reason: Correct meaning (growing on rocks or in rock crevices). The position parent matches its siblings epiphytic, terrestrial and aquatic (FLOPO:0991110-0991112). The synonyms lithophytic, rupestral, epilithic and rupicole fit.

label: semiovate
reason: Standard meaning of half-ovate (one half of an ovate outline, cut lengthwise), and the definition is well formed. PATO has only semicircular (PATO:0002232).

label: root-climbing
reason: Correct: the plant climbs by clinging with adventitious roots along the stem (e.g. ivy, many Araceae). It is properly placed under climbing (FLOPO:0991108).

label: unistratose
reason: Correct bryological usage (a lamina or margin one cell thick). Being one layer thick fits under PATO 'unstratified' (lacking a layered configuration). Monostratose is a correct synonym.

label: pseudolateral
reason: This is the standard Cyperaceae/Juncaceae usage: a terminal inflorescence pushed aside by a lowest bract that looks like the stem continued. PATO has nothing equivalent.

label: bipinnatipartite
reason: Correct, and it follows the pinnatipartite parent's pattern (twice pinnately parted).

label: cladautoicous
reason: Correct bryological meaning: male structures on their own short branch of the same plant, as against gonioautoicous (bud-like in a leaf axil). It is properly placed under autoicous.

label: induplicate
reason: The definition covers both standard uses: induplicate-valvate aestivation (margins folded inward) and induplicate (V-shaped) folding of palm leaves. Folded is a suitable parent.

label: rhizome-like
definition: A shape quality inhering in a bearer by virtue of the bearer's resembling a rhizome in form: an elongate, thickened, more or less cylindrical axis, often bearing scale leaves or nodes.
reason: The current text puts position and habit ('horizontal, usually subterranean') into a shape quality. Those belong to a separate position or orientation quality. Keep only what is about form.

label: obtrapeziform
reason: Correct 'ob-' inversion of trapeziform (the wider parallel side at the apex), properly placed under PATO:0002044 trapezoid.

label: pleiochasial
reason: Correct: a cyme with more than two branches below each terminal flower, as against dichasial and monochasial. Branched is a suitable parent, and polychasial is an exact synonym.

label: intramarginal
reason: Correct for intramarginal veins and sori (just inside the margin and running along it). PATO has no such term.

label: collateral
reason: Correct standard meaning (side by side at the same level, e.g. collateral ovules or collateral buds). The ovule example helps.

label: gynobasic
reason: Correct (Lamiaceae and Boraginaceae: the style arises from the base between the ovary lobes). The stamen and spike bearers look like extraction noise but do not affect the class.

label: accumbent
reason: Correct Brassicaceae meaning: the radicle lies against the edges of the cotyledons, as against incumbent, where it lies against the back of one cotyledon.

label: paracytic
reason: Matches the standard stomatal-type definition (subsidiary cells parallel to the guard cells). 'Rubiaceous' is correctly only a related synonym.

label: drupe-like
reason: The exact synonym 'drupaceous' does not fit. In floras it is used for true drupes as often as for drupe-like fruits, while this definition excludes true drupes. Make 'drupaceous' a related synonym. The definition is otherwise sound.

label: hemiparasitic
definition: A parasitic quality inhering in a plant by virtue of its being green and photosynthetic while drawing water and mineral nutrients from a host plant through haustoria.
reason: Wrong parent. FLOPO:0991265 'parasitic' (trophic quality, 'wholly or in part') now exists, and hemiparasitic is a kind of it. The definition text is correct.

label: decompound
reason: Correct glossary meaning (divided or compound more than once, e.g. bi- or tripinnate leaves, repeatedly branched panicles). PATO has no compound or decompound value.
